In the summer of 1965 the astronauts carried a hand-held camera into orbit almost as an afterthought. Nobody expected much; the cameras were there to document the mission, and the real work was supposed to be navigation and rendezvous. But when the crew looked out the window they saw the world unrolling beneath them, clouds spiraling over oceans, the Nile threading through the desert like a green wire, and they began to shoot. By the end of the flight they had hundreds of frames. Back on the ground, scientists crowded around the prints, astonished at what they showed: coastlines, storms, and mountain ranges seen whole. The photographs convinced a skeptical agency that the view from orbit had real scientific value, and within a few years Earth observation was a formal program.
